title: Adjacency matrices and walks
summary: An [[adjacency-matrix|adjacency matrix]] stores a graph as a grid of numbers, and its powers count [[walk|walks]]: entry $(i, j)$ of $A^{k}$ is the number of walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$. You also use [[weighted-adjacency-table|weighted adjacency tables]] and build the [[transition-matrix|transition matrix]] behind Google's PageRank.

goals.text: Write the adjacency matrix of a graph, and read a graph from its [[matrix|matrix]].
Describe a walk and its length.
Count walks of exactly $k$, or at most $k$, edges with powers of the adjacency matrix, and decide which vertices can be reached.
Use a weighted adjacency table of costs, distances or times.
Construct the transition matrix for a random walk on a [[strongly-connected-graph|strongly connected graph]], as in PageRank.

synonyms: number of walks of length k

before.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 5\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the element in row $2$, column $2$ of $AB$.
before.hint: Multiply row 2 of $A$ by column 2 of $B$, term by term, and add.

before.prompt: A [[directed-graph|directed graph]] has edges J → K, J → L, J → M, K → L, L → J and M → L. What is the in-degree of L?
before.hint: Count only the arrows that end at L.
before.explain: J → L, K → L and M → L end at L, so the in-degree is $3$. Revise it in {{lesson:3.14}}.

blocks.text: A drawing of a graph is easy to read but hard to calculate with. An adjacency matrix holds the same information as numbers.

blocks.statement: For a [[graph|graph]] with $n$ [[graph-vertex|vertices]], the [[adjacency-matrix|adjacency matrix]] $A$ is the $n \times n$ matrix whose entry $a_{ij}$, in row $i$ and column $j$, is the number of [[graph-edge|edges]] going directly from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$.
blocks.plain: Row is where you start, column is where you go.

blocks.text: Label the rows and columns in the same order, usually alphabetical. A $0$ means no direct edge, and two separate edges give a $2$.

Undirected graph: each edge works both ways, so $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ and the matrix is symmetric about the leading diagonal. With no loops, each row adds up to the [[degree-of-a-vertex|degree]] of its vertex.
[[directed-graph|Directed graph]]: an edge from $i$ to $j$ adds $1$ to row $i$, column $j$ only. Rows add up to out-degrees and columns to in-degrees.
A loop at $i$ puts $1$ on the leading diagonal: going round it is one step from $i$ back to $i$. A [[simple-graph|simple graph]] has only $0$s and $1$s, with $0$s on the diagonal.

blocks.alt: An undirected graph with five vertices F, G, K, L and V. Edges: F to G, F to K, F to L, G to K, K to L, K to V and L to V.
blocks.caption: Paths in a park between the fountain F, gate G, kiosk K, lake L and viewpoint V.

blocks.question: Write down the adjacency matrix $A$ for the park paths in the figure. Use the order F, G, K, L, V.
steps: F is joined to G, K and L, so row F is $0, 1, 1, 1, 0$. G is joined to F and K: $1, 0, 1, 0, 0$.
K is joined to F, G, L and V: $1, 1, 0, 1, 1$. L to F, K and V: $1, 0, 1, 0, 1$. V to K and L: $0, 0, 1, 1, 0$.
Check: $A$ is symmetric with $0$s on the diagonal. The row sums $3, 2, 4, 3, 2$ add to $14 = 2 \times 7$, matching the $7$ paths.

blocks.alt: A directed graph with four vertices P, Q, R and S. Arrows: P to Q and Q to P (two separate edges), Q to R, R to S, S to P, and R to P along the diagonal.
blocks.caption: Lifts and runs in a ski area. The gondola between P and Q runs both ways; every other link is one way.

blocks.question: Each arrow in the ski area is a lift or a run, used only in its direction. Write down its adjacency matrix $M$ (order P, Q, R, S). How many lifts and runs arrive at P?
steps: Rows are “from”, columns are “to”. Row P: $0, 1, 0, 0$. Row Q: $1, 0, 1, 0$. Row R: $1, 0, 0, 1$. Row S: $1, 0, 0, 0$.
$M$ is not symmetric: row R, column S is $1$ but row S, column R is $0$, because the run from R to S is one way.
Column P adds to $3$, the in-degree of P. In context: a skier can reach P directly from Q, R or S, but there is only one way out of P.

blocks.text: “Write down the adjacency matrix”: label rows and columns, or state the order. For a directed graph, say that rows are “from”.

blocks.prompt: An undirected graph with no loops has adjacency matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 & 0\\1 & 0 & 1 & 1\\2 & 1 & 0 & 1\\0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. How many edges does it have?
blocks.hint: Each edge appears twice in the matrix.
blocks.explain: The entries add to $12$. Each edge is counted twice, so there are $6$ edges, two of them between the first and third vertices.

blocks.prompt: In the adjacency matrix of a directed graph, rows are “from”. What does the sum of row Q give?
blocks.hint: Every entry in row Q counts edges that start at Q.

options.text: The out-degree of Q
The in-degree of Q
The degree of Q, counted twice
The number of vertices that can reach Q

blocks.explain: Row Q counts the edges leaving Q, so it adds up to the out-degree. Column Q gives the in-degree.

sections.heading: Walks and powers of the adjacency matrix

blocks.statement: A [[walk|walk]] is a sequence of edges in which each edge starts at the vertex where the previous edge ended. Vertices and edges may repeat. Its length is the number of edges.
blocks.plain: A journey along edges, where going back over old ground is allowed.

blocks.text: Write a walk as a list of vertices. F–K–L–K has length $3$ and visits K twice. In a directed graph a walk follows the arrows. {{lesson:3.16}} adds trails, which never repeat an edge, and paths, which never repeat a vertex.
Count the walks of length $2$ from $i$ to $j$. Each is $i \to m \to j$ for some middle vertex $m$, and there are $a_{im}a_{mj}$ of them through $m$.
Adding over every $m$ gives $a_{i1}a_{1j} + \dots + a_{in}a_{nj}$: row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $A$. That is entry $(i, j)$ of $A^{2}$.

blocks.statement: If $A$ is the adjacency matrix of a graph, entry $(i, j)$ of $A^{k}$ (row $i$, column $j$) is the number of walks of length $k$ from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$.
blocks.why: $A^{k} = A^{k-1}A$, so each extra factor of $A$ adds one step, counted by the same row-times-column sum.

blocks.text: The leading diagonal of $A^{k}$ counts closed walks: entry $(i, i)$ counts the walks of length $k$ from $i$ back to $i$.

blocks.question: Without a calculator, use the park matrix $A$ to find the number of walks of length $2$ from F to V. List them to check.
steps: You need entry (F, V) of $A^{2}$: row F of $A$ times column V of $A$.
The non-zero products come from K and L, so the walks are F–K–V and F–L–V, as in the figure.

blocks.question: A skier starts at Q, uses exactly $6$ lifts or runs and finishes at P. Use your calculator to find the number of possible walks, and write down one.
steps: Write down what you need: entry (Q, P) of $M^{6}$. This earns the method mark.
Enter $M$ in the order P, Q, R, S and find $M^{6} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2 & 2 & 1\\5 & 4 & 2 & 2\\4 & 3 & 2 & 1\\2 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Row Q, column P is $5$.
One walk is Q–R–P–Q–R–S–P. It uses the lift from Q to R twice, which a walk allows.

blocks.prompt: For the ski area, $M^{4} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 & 0\\2 & 2 & 1 & 1\\2 & 1 & 1 & 1\\1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ (order P, Q, R, S). Can a skier go from P to S using exactly $4$ lifts or runs?
blocks.hint: Row is the start and column is the finish.

options.text: No: row P, column S is 0
Yes: row S, column P is 1
Yes: row P has non-zero entries
No: there is no arrow from P to S

blocks.explain: Walks from P to S are in row P, column S, which is $0$. Row S, column P counts walks from S to P. A missing direct arrow says nothing about walks of length $4$.

verify.truth: No: row P, column S is 0

blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to find $A^{3}$ for the park. How many walks of length $3$ start and end at the same place, counting all five places?
blocks.explain: The diagonal is $4, 2, 6, 4, 2$, which adds to $18$. Each goes round a triangle of paths, such as F–G–K–F.

sections.heading: Walks of at most k edges, and reaching every vertex

blocks.text: When any number of edges up to a limit is allowed, add the counts for each length.

blocks.tex: \text{walks of length } 1 \text{ to } k \text{ from } i \text{ to } j = \text{entry } (i, j) \text{ of } A + A^{2} + \dots + A^{k}

blocks.text: “At most $k$” means lengths $1$ to $k$. “Fewer than $k$” stops at $k - 1$.

A $0$ in entry $(i, j)$ of $A^{k}$ means no walk of exactly $k$ edges goes from $i$ to $j$. If every entry off the leading diagonal of $A + A^{2} + \dots + A^{k}$ is non-zero, every vertex can reach every other in at most $k$ steps.

blocks.question: Find the number of walks from G to V in the park that use at most $3$ paths.
steps: Add entry (G, V) of $A$, $A^{2}$ and $A^{3}$: $0 + 1 + 3$.
These are G–K–V, then G–F–K–V, G–F–L–V and G–K–L–V.
In context: there are $4$ ways from the gate to the viewpoint along at most three paths.

blocks.question: For the ski area, use $M + M^{2}$ and $M + M^{2} + M^{3}$ to decide whether a skier can get from every point to every other using (a) at most $2$, (b) at most $3$ lifts or runs.
steps: (a) $M + M^{2} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 0\\2 & 1 & 1 & 1\\2 & 1 & 0 & 1\\1 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Off the diagonal, row S, column R is $0$ (and so is row P, column S).
So no: there is no walk of $1$ or $2$ edges from S to R.

(b) $M + M^{2} + M^{3} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 2 & 1 & 1\\4 & 2 & 2 & 1\\3 & 2 & 1 & 1\\2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. Every entry off the leading diagonal is non-zero, so yes. For example, S to R is S–P–Q–R.
The $0$ in row S, column S only means a skier can't return to S within $3$ steps.
blocks.answer: (a) No: no walk from S to R. (b) Yes: every entry off the leading diagonal of $M + M^{2} + M^{3}$ is non-zero.

verify.truth: At most 2: no (S to R impossible); at most 3: yes, no zero off the diagonal of M + M^2 + M^3

blocks.prompt: You need the number of walks from X to Y with fewer than $4$ edges. Which matrix do you read?
blocks.hint: Is a walk of length 4 allowed?
blocks.explain: Fewer than $4$ edges means lengths $1$, $2$ and $3$. $A^{3}$ alone counts only walks of exactly $3$ edges.

blocks.prompt: $M + M^{2} + M^{3}$ has a $0$ in row E, column B, and no other zeros off the leading diagonal. Which is correct?
blocks.hint: Row is the start, and the sum covers walks of up to 3 edges.

options.text: You can't get from E to B in 3 steps or fewer
You can't get from B to E in 3 steps or fewer
Every vertex can reach every other in 3 steps or fewer
You can't get from E to B at all

blocks.explain: Row E, column B counts walks from E to B of length 1 to 3. A longer walk might still exist, so “at all” goes too far.

verify.truth: You can't get from E to B in 3 steps or fewer

blocks.statement: A [[weighted-adjacency-table|weighted adjacency table]] for a [[weighted-graph|weighted graph]] has a row and a column for each vertex. Entry $(i, j)$ is the weight of the direct edge from $i$ to $j$, such as a cost, distance or time, and is blank (or –) when there is no direct edge.
blocks.plain: An adjacency matrix with weights in place of the 1s.

blocks.text: Never write $0$ for a missing edge: $0$ would mean a link that is free or instant. Undirected weights give a symmetric table; for directed weights, rows are “from”.
The table shows only direct edges, so the cheapest way between two vertices may go through others. Raising a table of weights to a power doesn't count walks.

blocks.question: Crossing times, in minutes, between five islands are shown; – means no direct ferry. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} & \mathrm{V} & \mathrm{W} & \mathrm{X} & \mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{Z} \\ \hline \mathrm{V} & \text{–} & 25 & 40 & \text{–} & \text{–} \\ \mathrm{W} & 25 & \text{–} & 10 & 32 & \text{–} \\ \mathrm{X} & 40 & 10 & \text{–} & 20 & 55 \\ \mathrm{Y} & \text{–} & 32 & 20 & \text{–} & 15 \\ \mathrm{Z} & \text{–} & \text{–} & 55 & 15 & \text{–} \end{array}$ (a) Draw the weighted graph. (b) Ignoring waiting times, find the quickest journey time from V to Z.
steps: (a) One vertex per island, and one edge for each entry above the leading diagonal, labelled with its time (figure below).
(b) Quickest to X: V–W–X $= 35$, less than V–X $= 40$. Quickest to Y: V–W–X–Y $= 55$, less than V–W–Y $= 57$ or V–X–Y $= 60$.
Z is reached from Y ($15$) or X ($55$): $55 + 15 = 70$ beats $35 + 55 = 90$. So V–W–X–Y–Z takes $70$ minutes.
Interpret: the quickest journey uses four ferries. Waiting at each change could make a route with fewer ferries better in practice.

blocks.alt: A weighted graph with five vertices V, W, X, Y and Z. Edge weights in minutes: V to W 25, V to X 40, W to X 10, W to Y 32, X to Y 20, X to Z 55 and Y to Z 15.
blocks.caption: The ferry table as a weighted graph, in minutes. Not to scale.

blocks.question: Cycling times, in minutes, between three hillside villages are shown, rows as the start. $\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{from} \backslash \text{to} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{G} & \mathrm{H} \\ \hline \mathrm{F} & \text{–} & 18 & 30 \\ \mathrm{G} & 12 & \text{–} & 14 \\ \mathrm{H} & 22 & 9 & \text{–} \end{array}$ (a) Explain why the table is not symmetric. (b) A cyclist leaves F, visits G and H, and returns to F. Find the shorter total time.
steps: (a) Uphill is slower than downhill, so times depend on direction: F to H takes $30$ minutes, H to F only $22$.
So F–H–G–F, $51$ minutes: it does the slow climb to H early and freewheels down to G.

blocks.prompt: In a weighted table of bus fares, row B, column D is blank. What does this mean?
blocks.hint: The table only shows direct links.

options.text: No direct bus runs from B to D
The bus from B to D is free
You can't get from B to D by bus
The fare is the same both ways

blocks.explain: A blank means no direct edge; you may still get there by changing. A free bus would be written $0$.

verify.truth: No direct bus runs from B to D

blocks.prompt: An inspector sails every ferry route in the island table once. Find the total crossing time, in minutes.
blocks.hint: Add only the entries above the leading diagonal.
blocks.explain: $25 + 40 + 10 + 32 + 20 + 55 + 15 = 197$. The whole table gives $394$, counting every route twice.

sections.heading: Transition matrices for a random walk

blocks.text: Picture a visitor who keeps moving along an edge chosen at random. A transition matrix holds the probability of each move.

blocks.statement: For a [[strongly-connected-graph|strongly connected]] directed graph, or a connected undirected graph, the [[transition-matrix|transition matrix]] $T$ has $T_{ij}$ = the probability of moving from vertex $j$ to vertex $i$. In a simple graph with equally likely edges, $T_{ij} = \frac{1}{\text{out-degree of } j}$ if there is an edge from $j$ to $i$, and $0$ otherwise.
blocks.plain: Each column is where you are now, sharing a probability of 1 equally between its edges out.

blocks.text: For an undirected graph, the out-degree is the degree. Each column adds up to $1$. Columns are “from”, as in {{lesson:4.19}}: the other way round from $A$, so $T$ is $A$ transposed with each column divided by its total.
The graph must be strongly connected: a vertex with no edge out would give a column of zeros, and a walker could get stuck in one part of the graph.

blocks.alt: An undirected graph with four vertices A, B, C and D. Edges: A to B, A to C, B to C and C to D.
blocks.caption: Four museum rooms; each edge is a doorway.

blocks.question: A visitor moves round the museum rooms, each time choosing a doorway of their room at random. Construct the transition matrix $T$ (order A, B, C, D).
steps: Column A: B and C each get $\frac{1}{2}$. Column B: A and C each get $\frac{1}{2}$. Column C: A, B and D each get $\frac{1}{3}$. Column D: C gets $1$.
Check: each column adds up to $1$. Interpret: row C, column D is $1$ because D's only doorway leads to C.

blocks.text: Google's PageRank works this way. Pages are vertices and links are directed edges. A surfer clicks a random link on each page, and the pages visited most in the long run rank highest. The full algorithm also adds random jumps; {{lesson:4.19}} finds the long-run proportions.

blocks.alt: A directed graph with four vertices H, N, S and W. Arrows: H to N and N to H, H to S and S to H (each pair as two separate edges), N to S, H to W, and W to S.
blocks.caption: Links between four web pages: home H, news N, sport S and weather W.

blocks.question: A surfer clicks one of the links on their page at random. Construct the transition matrix $T$ for the website (order H, N, S, W).
steps: Out-degrees: H $3$ (to N, S, W), N $2$ (to H, S), S $1$ (to H), W $1$ (to S). Every page can reach every other, so the graph is strongly connected.
Column H: N, S, W each $\frac{1}{3}$. Column N: H, S each $\frac{1}{2}$. Column S: H gets $1$. Column W: S gets $1$.
Interpret: S has the most links in, but it passes every visitor to H. In the long run the surfer is on H about $40\%$ of the time and on S about $33\%$: links from a busy page count for more.

blocks.text: Building $T$ with rows as “from”. In IB transition matrices each column is the starting vertex, so columns add up to $1$.

blocks.prompt: Which is true for every column of the transition matrix of a strongly connected graph?
blocks.hint: A column lists every possible move from one vertex.

options.text: Its entries add up to 1
Its entries add up to the degree
It equals the matching row
It has one non-zero entry

blocks.explain: From any vertex the walker must move somewhere, so the column adds to $1$. Rows usually differ, as in the museum matrix.

blocks.prompt: A surfer starts on page H. Find the probability that they are on page S after exactly $2$ clicks.
blocks.hint: List the 2-click walks from H to S and multiply the probabilities along each.
blocks.explain: H–N–S: $\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{6}$. H–W–S: $\frac{1}{3}$. Total $\frac{1}{2}$, which is entry (S, H) of $T^{2}$.

blocks.text: Adjacency matrix: entry $(i, j)$ is the number of edges directly from $i$ to $j$. Symmetric for an undirected graph; for a directed graph, rows are “from”.
A walk is a sequence of edges, each starting where the last ended; vertices and edges may repeat. Its length is its number of edges.

blocks.tex: \text{entry } (i, j) \text{ of } A^{k} = \text{number of walks of length } k \text{ from } i \text{ to } j
\text{walks of length } 1 \text{ to } k \text{ from } i \text{ to } j = \text{entry } (i, j) \text{ of } A + A^{2} + \dots + A^{k}

blocks.text: The leading diagonal of $A^{k}$ counts closed walks of length $k$. No zero off the diagonal of $A + \dots + A^{k}$ means every vertex reaches every other in at most $k$ steps.
Weighted adjacency table: entries are weights of direct edges; blank (not $0$) means no direct edge.

Transition matrix of a strongly connected directed graph, or a connected undirected one: $T_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from $j$ to $i$, so columns add to $1$. With equally likely edges in a simple graph, $T_{ij} = \frac{1}{\text{out-degree of } j}$ when $j \to i$ is an edge, and $0$ otherwise.

mistakes: A matrix of the wrong size or with no labels. $n$ vertices give an $n \times n$ matrix; label the rows and columns.
Reading the wrong entry. Row is the start, so walks from E to B are in row E, column B.
Using $A^{k}$ alone when shorter walks count. “At most $k$” needs $A + \dots + A^{k}$; “fewer than $k$” stops at $A^{k-1}$.
Treating walks as real routes. A walk can pass its end vertex early or repeat edges, so if the journey must stop at the target, the true count may be smaller.
examTips: “Find the number of walks”: write the entry you need, such as “row Q, column P of $M^{6}$”, before the number. That earns the method mark.
“State, with justification” whether every vertex can be reached: quote the zero or non-zero entries and say what they mean, such as “no walk from S to R in $2$ steps”.
“Hence”: use your own matrix from the earlier part. A wrong matrix used correctly can still earn follow-through marks.
